stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with at least three distinct zeros, and let $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)$. Prove that $g$ has at least three distinct zeros. [10 marks]
answer: Every zero of $f$ is a zero of $g$; in fact the zero sets coincide.
solution: Since $e^{x/2}>0$ for every real $x$, $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)=0$ iff $f(x)=0$. Thus the three distinct zeros of $f$ remain three distinct zeros of $g$.
hint: The exponential factor never vanishes.

stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with at least three distinct zeros, and let $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)$. Prove that $f+2f'$ has at least two distinct zeros. [20 marks]
answer: Apply Rolle's theorem to $g$ between consecutive zeros.
solution: Choose three distinct zeros $a<b<c$ of $f$, and hence of $g$. Since $g$ is continuously differentiable, Rolle's theorem gives $u\in(a,b)$ and $v\in(b,c)$ such that $g'(u)=g'(v)=0$. These points are distinct. Differentiating gives $g'(x)=\frac12e^{x/2}[f(x)+2f'(x)]$. The prefactor is nonzero, so $f(u)+2f'(u)=f(v)+2f'(v)=0$.
hint: Differentiate $e^{x/2}f(x)$ and use Rolle's theorem on two disjoint intervals.

stem: Find all solutions of $\max(x^2+y^2)$ subject to $x+y\leq1$ and $x,y\geq0$. [12 marks]
answer: Maximum value1, attained only at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
solution: For nonnegative $x,y$, $x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2-2xy\leq(x+y)^2\leq1$. Equality requires both $x+y=1$ and $xy=0$, yielding exactly $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. No other feasible point attains1.
hint: Compare $x^2+y^2$ with $(x+y)^2$ and track equality conditions.

stem: In the fictional puzzle, 1000 senators each bring one bottle of wine to a king. Exactly one bottle is poisoned, indistinguishable in advance. There are10 prisoner taste testers. The poison's binary outcome appears exactly24hours later, and there is time for only one round of tests. How can the poisoned bottle be identified with certainty? [18 marks]
answer: Encode bottle labels in10 binary digits; the10 test outcomes identify the label, since $2^{10}=1024\geq1000$.
solution: As an abstract coding problem, label the bottles0 through999 and write each label as a10-bit binary word. Associate one tester with each bit position. The test for bit position $j$ combines samples from exactly those bottle labels whose $j$th bit is1. In the puzzle's assumptions, after24hours the positive/negative outcome of each test states whether the unique poisoned label has that bit equal to1 or0. Read the ten outcomes as a binary integer to recover the unique bottle. The all-zero label corresponds to all-negative outcomes, which is still informative because exactly one poisoned bottle is assumed. Ten bits distinguish1024 possibilities; nine bits distinguish only512, so ten binary tests are also the minimum needed in one round.
hint: Use binary information rather than assigning one tester to one bottle.
notes: Presented strictly as the source fictional binary-coding puzzle; no real-world poison preparation or exposure information is involved.

stem: Let matrices $A,B$ have a defined product $AB$. Prove that if the columns of $B$ are linearly dependent, then the columns of $AB$ are linearly dependent. [15 marks]
answer: A nonzero vector $z$ satisfying $Bz=0$ also satisfies $(AB)z=0$.
solution: Column dependence of $B$ means there exists a nonzero coefficient vector $z$ such that $Bz=0$. Multiplying by $A$ gives $(AB)z=A(Bz)=0$. The same nonzero coefficients form a vanishing linear combination of columns of $AB$, proving their dependence. No invertibility assumption on $A$ is needed.
hint: Express column dependence as a nontrivial null-vector equation.

stem: Let $e_i$ be the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb R^3$. A linear map $L:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfies $L(e_1)=e_1$, $L(e_2)=e_1+e_2$ and $L(e_3)=e_2+e_3$. Is $L$ onto? Prove your answer. [15 marks]
answer: Yes. Its matrix is upper triangular with determinant1.
solution: The columns of the matrix of $L$ are its values on the standard basis: $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. It is upper triangular with determinant1, hence invertible and onto. Explicitly, for a desired image $(a,b,c)$ choose input $(a-b+c,b-c,c)$; multiplication by $M$ gives $(a,b,c)$.
hint: Place the images of the basis vectors in the columns of the representing matrix.

stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. Graphically depict the consumer's equilibrium. [10 marks]
answer: The optimum is a tangency on the steeper post-quota budget segment, with marginal rate of substitution equal to the market price.
solution: Let income be $m$ and let the other consumption good have price1. With total rice $x$ on the horizontal axis and other consumption $y$ on the vertical axis, the budget frontier is $y=m-p_sx$ for $0\leq x\leq q$, then $y=m+(p-p_s)q-px$ for $x\geq q$. It is continuous at the kink $(q,m-p_sq)$ and becomes steeper there, changing slope from $-p_s$ to $-p$. By the given assumption, the optimum lies strictly to the right of the kink on the second segment, at a tangency with the highest attainable indifference curve. The absolute slope of that curve, $MRS_{x,y}$, equals $p$, and open-market purchases are $x-q>0$.
hint: Draw a budget line that becomes steeper once the low-price quota is exhausted.

stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. Suppose rice is normal. What happens to the amount purchased from the open market if the ration quota is cut? Explain. [10 marks]
answer: Total rice consumption falls, but the change in open-market purchases is not determined by normality of rice alone. With both goods normal, open-market purchases rise.
solution: While the consumer remains beyond the kink, the relevant budget is equivalent to income $M=m+(p-p_s)q$ at marginal rice price $p$. Let total Marshallian rice demand be $x(p,M)$ and open-market purchases $z=x-q$. A quota cut lowers $M$, so normality implies total rice $x$ falls. But $dz/dq=(p-p_s)x_M-1$: the quota itself is also falling, so the sign of the change in $z$ is ambiguous unless the strength of the income effect is bounded. If $0<x_M<1/(p-p_s)$, a cut in $q$ raises open-market purchases; if $x_M>1/(p-p_s)$, it lowers them. Under the additional usual assumption that both rice and the other good are normal, budget differentiation gives $px_M<1$, implying the first case and higher open-market purchases. Normality of rice alone does not impose that bound when the other good may be inferior.
hint: Distinguish total rice from open-market rice: the latter equals total demand minus the ration quota.
notes: The source assumes only rice normal, not the other good. An unconditional increase in open-market purchases would require an additional bound on the rice income effect. The answer states both the general ambiguity and the standard both-normal-goods case.

stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. If rice is normal, what happens to open-market purchases when the subsidised price rises but remains below the market price? Does the conclusion change if rice is inferior? Explain. [10 marks]
answer: Normal rice: open-market purchases fall. Inferior rice: they rise, as long as the consumer continues to use the open-market segment.
solution: With the quota unchanged, increasing $p_s$ lowers the effective income $M=m+(p-p_s)q$ while leaving the marginal price $p$ unchanged. Thus $dx/dp_s=-q x_M$. For normal rice $x_M>0$, total rice falls and so do open-market purchases $z=x-q$; purchases may reach zero at the quota kink. If rice is inferior, $x_M<0$, the income loss instead raises total rice demand and open-market purchases. There is no substitution effect at the margin on the post-quota segment because the open-market marginal price is unchanged.
hint: A higher subsidised price changes the cost of the fixed quota, acting like a change in income for an open-market buyer.

stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. Derive marginal and average revenue per boat. [5 marks]
solution: Differentiate total revenue to get $MR=R'(x)=10{,}000(4-x)$. Divide revenue by the number of boats to get $AR=R(x)/x=10{,}000(4-x/2)$ for $x>0$.
hint: Differentiate total revenue for MR, and divide by boat numbers for AR.

stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. If fishing permits are allocated freely, how many boats fish each month? [10 marks]
answer: Four boats under free-entry/open-access equilibrium.
solution: With unrestricted free entry, each boat receives average revenue. Entry continues while $AR$ exceeds the hiring cost20,000. Zero net return requires $40{,}000-5{,}000x=20{,}000$, hence $x=4$. Total revenue80,000 then exactly covers the four boats' total real cost80,000.
hint: Open access equates average revenue, not marginal revenue, with cost per boat.

stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. How many boats maximize total profit? [5 marks]
answer: Two boats; maximum pre-permit resource profit is20,000rupees.
solution: Joint profit is $R(x)-20{,}000x=20{,}000x-5{,}000x^2$. It is a concave quadratic maximized at $x=2$, where marginal revenue equals the real boat cost20,000. Total revenue is60,000 and total hiring cost is40,000, leaving20,000.
hint: A joint owner accounts for the reduction in existing boats' catch when another boat enters.

stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. What per-boat permit charge induces the total-profit-maximizing number of boats? [10 marks]
answer: Charge10,000rupees per boat per month.
solution: At the desired $x=2$, average revenue per boat is $AR(2)=30{,}000$. Free entry with a permit charge $t$ equates this to $20{,}000+t$, giving $t=10{,}000$. The permit absorbs the congestion rent and implements two boats rather than four. The two permits raise20,000 for the municipality, equal to the maximized resource rent; permit payments are transfers, so private net boat profits are zero under free entry even though total pre-transfer resource surplus is maximized.
hint: Choose the fee so that average revenue at two boats equals hiring cost plus permit cost.

stem: A monopoly campus theatre has faculty demand $Q_F=500-4P_F$ and student demand $Q_S=100-2P_S$, with each demand truncated at zero. Capacity is sufficient for everyone. The total cost of servicing demand is500. If both groups must face the same price, find the profit-maximizing ticket price. [15 marks]
answer: Uniform price62.5, serving250faculty tickets and no student tickets; profit15,125.
solution: At a common price $p\leq50$, aggregate demand is $600-6p$ and revenue is $600p-6p^2$, maximized over this interval at $p=50$ with revenue15,000. At $50\leq p\leq125$, students buy zero and faculty demand is $500-4p$. Revenue $500p-4p^2$ is maximized at $p=62.5$, giving quantity250 and revenue15,625. This exceeds the best revenue from the lower-price segment. Subtracting the fixed cost500 gives profit15,125. Ignoring the student choke price would incorrectly select50 as the global optimum.
hint: Aggregate demand is kinked at the student choke price50; maximize revenue on both segments.
notes: The source states a total servicing cost of500, treated as fixed rather than a marginal cost of500 per ticket.

stem: A monopoly campus theatre has faculty demand $Q_F=500-4P_F$ and student demand $Q_S=100-2P_S$, with each demand truncated at zero. Capacity is sufficient for everyone. The total cost of servicing demand is500. If different prices can be charged to faculty and students, find the profit-maximizing prices. [15 marks]
answer: Faculty price62.5, student price25; total profit16,375.
solution: With zero marginal servicing cost and a fixed total cost, maximize the two group revenues separately. Faculty revenue $p_F(500-4p_F)$ has first-order condition $500-8p_F=0$, giving $p_F=62.5$ and $Q_F=250$. Student revenue $p_S(100-2p_S)$ gives $100-4p_S=0$, so $p_S=25$ and $Q_S=50$. Revenues are15,625 and1,250, respectively. Combined profit is $15{,}625+1{,}250-500=16{,}375$.
hint: Separate the two revenue-maximization problems; the common fixed cost does not alter either optimal price.

stem: In a Solow economy, $Y(t)=K(t)^\alpha L(t)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with both factors fully employed. Labour grows at rate $\eta>0$. A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. If initially $k(0)<k^*$, compare initial aggregate-output growth $g_Y(0)$ with steady-state output growth. Prove the comparison. [20 marks]
solution: Capital per worker obeys $\dot k=sk^\alpha-\eta k$, so $k^*=(s/\eta)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. Log differentiation of production gives $g_Y=\alpha g_K+(1-\alpha)\eta=\alpha s k^{\alpha-1}+(1-\alpha)\eta$. At $k^*$, $s(k^*)^{\alpha-1}=\eta$, giving $g_Y^*=\eta$. Since $\alpha-1<0$, $k(0)<k^*$ implies $sk(0)^{\alpha-1}>\eta$. Substitution yields $g_Y(0)>\eta$.
hint: Derive $g_Y$ in terms of capital per worker, noting that its exponent $\alpha-1$ is negative.

stem: In a Solow economy, $Y(t)=K(t)^\alpha L(t)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with both factors fully employed. Labour grows at rate $\eta>0$. A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. Compare the initial output-growth rates in two scenarios $k(0)<k'(0)<k^*$ for the same economy. [5 marks]
answer: The lower-capital scenario grows faster: $g_Y(k(0))>g_Y(k'(0))>\eta$.
solution: The formula from part(i) is $g_Y(k)=\alpha s k^{\alpha-1}+(1-\alpha)\eta$. Its derivative with respect to $k$ is $\alpha s(\alpha-1)k^{\alpha-2}<0$. Thus output growth is strictly higher at the lower initial capital per worker; both rates exceed their common steady-state rate because both initial stocks are below $k^*$.
hint: Use the monotonicity of the formula from part(i).

stem: In a Solow economy, $Y(t)=K(t)^\alpha L(t)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with both factors fully employed. Labour grows at rate $\eta>0$. A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. Two otherwise similarly described economies A and B have $s_A>s_B$. Their initial capital per worker is below their respective steady states. The printed condition is on aggregate capital: $K^A(0)<K^B(0)$. Can their initial output-growth rates be ranked? If the information is insufficient, say so. [5 marks]
answer: Insufficient information as printed: aggregate capital does not determine capital per worker without initial labour-force sizes.
solution: The ranking depends on $s_A[k_A(0)]^{\alpha-1}$ versus $s_B[k_B(0)]^{\alpha-1}$. Although $s_A>s_B$, the inequality $K_A(0)<K_B(0)$ does not order $k_A=K_A/L_A$ and $k_B=K_B/L_B$ without initial labour sizes. For example, take $\alpha=1/2$, $\eta=0.1$, $s_A=0.4$, $s_B=0.2$, $K_A=1<K_B=2$. The steady per-worker stocks are16 and4. If both initial per-worker stocks are1, A grows faster. But if $k_A=9$ and $k_B=1/4$ (achieved with different labour-force levels), both remain below their own steady states and B grows faster. Thus either ranking is possible. If the intended condition had instead been $k_A(0)<k_B(0)$, A would unambiguously grow faster, but that is not the printed aggregate-capital condition.
hint: Check carefully whether the source compares aggregate capital $K$ or capital per worker $k$.
notes: The user scan and matching official source both print uppercase aggregate K in the final assumption. This distinction is preserved rather than silently replacing it by lowercase k.

stem: What is the money multiplier, what determines it, and how is it related to monetary base and money supply? Which variables can the central bank change, and in which direction, to change money supply? [15 marks]
answer: In the textbook currency-deposit model, $M=mH$ with $m=(1+c)/(c+\rho)$, where $c=C/D$ and $\rho=Res/D$.
solution: Let currency be $C=cD$ and bank reserves $Res=\rho D$. Broad transaction money is $M=C+D=(1+c)D$ and monetary base is $H=C+Res=(c+\rho)D$. Thus $M=mH$, where $m=(1+c)/(c+\rho)$. More currency leakage or a higher reserve ratio reduces deposit creation; specifically $m_\rho<0$ and $m_c<0$ when $\rho<1$. The central bank can raise the monetary base through asset purchases or lending to banks, increasing money supply at a given multiplier; base contraction has the reverse effect. Lowering a binding reserve requirement can raise the multiplier and money supply, while raising it can reduce them. Currency preferences and excess reserves are behavioural rather than mechanically controlled, so the multiplier need not be constant or directly settable by the central bank. If using the question's reserve-to-assets terminology, the simple no-bank-equity balance-sheet model equates bank assets with deposits; otherwise the ratio must be converted to reserves per deposit before using this formula.
hint: Express both money and the monetary base as multiples of deposits.

stem: Why might the cash/deposit ratio and reserve/asset ratio fall when interest rises? How does an interest-sensitive money supply affect the LM curve compared with the standard LM? Explain the resulting effectiveness of counter-cyclical fiscal policy in a closed economy, using a diagram. [15 marks]
answer: Higher interest makes currency and excess reserves more costly to hold. The money multiplier rises with interest, making LM flatter and fiscal policy more effective.
solution: Holding cash forgoes interest on deposits or other assets, so a higher return can reduce the currency-deposit ratio. Likewise, higher lending or bond returns increase the opportunity cost of excess reserves, reducing the reserve ratio above any legal minimum. If both ratios decline, the multiplier $m(r)$ rises. With a fixed base $H$ and price level $P$, money equilibrium becomes $Hm(r)/P=L(Y,r)$, with $L_Y>0,L_r<0,m'(r)>0$. Its slope is $dr/dY=L_Y/[Hm'(r)/P-L_r]$, smaller than the fixed-money-supply slope $L_Y/(-L_r)$. Draw the standard upward-sloping LM and a flatter interest-sensitive LM through the same initial $(Y,r)$ point. A fiscal expansion shifts IS right; induced money expansion limits the interest rise and investment crowding-out, producing a larger output increase. The reverse applies to contraction. Required reserves and other balance-sheet restrictions limit the size of the response.
hint: Put the endogenous money supply on the left of the LM equilibrium and differentiate it with respect to income.

stem: Explain the difference between nominal and real exchange rates, with an example. Is a rise in the real cost of imports an improvement or deterioration in the terms of trade? [10 marks]
answer: A nominal rate exchanges currencies; a real rate compares goods prices. A higher real import cost is a deterioration in the terms of trade.
solution: Define $e$ as Home-currency units per Foreign-currency unit. It is a nominal exchange rate. The real exchange rate $q=eP^*/P$ compares the Home-currency price of a Foreign goods basket with the price of a Home basket. For a purely hypothetical example, if $e=80$, a Foreign basket costs10 Foreign units and a Home basket costs400 Home units, then $q=80\cdot10/400=2$: the imported basket costs two Home baskets. Terms of trade measure export prices relative to import prices. If imports become more expensive in real terms, more exports are needed to obtain a given quantity of imports, so the terms of trade deteriorate. Authors defining the exchange rate reciprocally reverse the numerical direction, but not this economic interpretation.
hint: Separate a currency conversion rate from the relative purchasing cost of goods, and state the quotation convention.

stem: A small open economy has a government budget surplus and a trade deficit. Identify the private sector's financial balance. Using the short-run Mundell-Fleming model with perfect capital mobility, explain how a sudden fall in private consumption affects output, the trade balance and the government budget under fixed and flexible exchange rates, including adjustment mechanisms. [20 marks]
answer: The private sector is in deficit. With a peg, output falls and the trade balance improves. With a float and fixed monetary base, depreciation offsets the demand fall, leaving output unchanged and improving the trade balance. Budget effects depend on tax rules.
solution:
The sectoral identity is $(S-I)+(T-G)=NX$. Since $T-G>0$ and $NX<0$, private net saving $S-I=NX-(T-G)<0$, so the private sector is in financial deficit.

Under fixed exchange rates, lower consumption shifts IS left and creates downward pressure on the domestic interest rate relative to the world rate. Capital outflow puts depreciation pressure on the currency. To defend the peg the central bank sells foreign reserves and contracts domestic money, shifting LM left. The new equilibrium has the world interest rate, lower output, and lower imports; net exports improve at the unchanged exchange rate. With income-dependent tax receipts the budget surplus shrinks as output falls; with fixed lump-sum taxes and fixed spending, the budget balance is unchanged.

Under flexible exchange rates with an unchanged monetary base and price level, the lower-consumption shock also creates capital outflow and depreciation pressure, but the central bank does not defend a peg. Depreciation raises net exports and shifts IS back until goods and money markets clear at the world interest rate. LM at that interest rate fixes output at its initial level, so the trade balance improves enough to offset the consumption loss while output is unchanged. The government budget is then unchanged under either fixed taxes or a tax rule depending only on unchanged income. These are the standard short-run model assumptions; an epidemic's additional supply effects are outside this specified consumption shock.
hint: Start from the sectoral-balance identity, then track how the exchange-rate regime determines the money-market adjustment.
notes: The source does not state a tax-revenue rule. Fixed-rate budget deterioration requires income-sensitive taxes; under the basic fixed-T,G version it is unchanged. Both cases are stated rather than imposing an unstated unique budget response.
